learningObjective: Understand how graph-level, tensor-expression-level, and loop-level IRs collaborate in a typical deep-learning compiler pipeline.
stem: In a typical deep learning compiler organized around three IR layers — graph-level (e.g., XLA HLO, TVM Relax), tensor-expression-level (e.g., linalg-on-tensor, TensorIR), and loop-level (affine, scf, low-level loop IR) — which statements are correct about their respective roles? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Compilers that use all three levels always require the user to author their program in the loop-level IR first; the graph and tensor layers are derived by structure-recovery passes that undo the loop nesting.

Tensor-expression-level IR expresses per-element computation via structured ops (e.g., linalg.generic) or explicit tensor expressions; it is the natural layer for tiling, vectorization decisions, and mapping to hardware intrinsics like tensor cores.
Loop-level IR makes iteration variables and memory accesses fully explicit, enabling low-level transformations (unrolling, software pipelining, register allocation) before codegen to LLVM/PTX.
Graph-level IR performs coarse-grained optimizations (op fusion, constant folding, layout choices, shape inference) treating ops as atomic; it does not itself expose loop structure.

explanation: The three-layer IR model is: (Graph) coarse-grained ops with shape/dtype; enables graph-level fusion, constant folding, layout, and shape inference. (Tensor) structured ops expressing per-element compute; the layer where tiling and hardware-intrinsic mapping fit naturally. (Loop) explicit loop nests and memory accesses; the layer where unrolling, vectorization, and register scheduling apply. Programs are authored at the graph (or framework) layer and lowered downward — not upward from loops.

optionExplanations.A: Wrong: authoring is at the graph/framework level; the flow is top-down (graph -> tensor -> loop).

assumptions: The compiler follows a common three-layer decomposition; some frameworks collapse or split further.
nonImplications: Does not imply every compiler must have exactly three layers; different projects choose different numbers of levels.
Does not imply that layers are strictly hierarchical without back-edges; some pipelines cross layers for iterative refinement.
